# Introduction

{{< include ../include/activate_environment.qmd >}}

Welcome to this tutorial on plotting in Julia! We'll be using the powerful Plots.jl package to create beautiful and informative visualizations. Don't worry if you're new to plotting – we'll start with the basics and gradually build up to more advanced techniques.

In this tutorial, you'll learn how to:
1. Create simple plots like line graphs and scatter plots
2. Customize your plots with colors, labels, and styles
3. Add multiple data series to a single plot
4. Save your plots as image files for use in reports or presentations
5. Give your plots a clear look that puts the data first

Follow the instructions, write your code in the designated code blocks, and validate your results with `@assert` statements.

Before we begin, let's make sure you have the necessary packages installed. If you've been following the course, you'll need to install the Plots and StatsPlots packages (StatsPlots adds statistical plot recipes like `boxplot`, which we will use at the end of this tutorial):

```{julia}
#| eval: false
#| output: false
import Pkg
Pkg.add(["Plots","StatsPlots"])
```

Now, let's load these packages:

```{julia}
#| eval: true
#| output: false
using Plots, StatsPlots
```

---

# Section 1 - Creating Basic Plots

The Plots.jl package simplifies the process of creating a wide array of plots, from simple line plots to complex 3D visualizations. Let's start with the simplest type of plot: a line plot. We'll create some example data and then plot it.

```{julia}
#| eval: true
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of 10 random values between 0 and 1 over x from 1 to 10, with the title My First Line Plot, labelled x and y axes and no legend."
# Create some example data
x = 1:10      # This creates a range of numbers from 1 to 10
y = rand(10)  # This creates 10 random numbers between 0 and 1

# Create a basic line plot
line_plot = plot(
    x, y,
    title="My First Line Plot",
    xlabel="X-axis Label",
    ylabel="Y-axis Label",
    legend=false
)

# Display the plot
display(line_plot)
```

Let's break down what each part of this code does:

- `plot(x, y, ...)` creates the plot using our x and y data
- `title=...` sets the title of the plot
- `xlabel=...` and `ylabel=...` label the x and y axes
- `legend=false` turns off the legend (we'll use this later)
- `display(line_plot)` shows the plot. When you run a cell, its last expression is displayed automatically, so this line is optional here - but you will need `display` when you create plots inside loops or functions later in the course.

::: {.callout-note}
We use random numbers in this tutorial, so your plots will look different from the ones shown here. That is expected and not a mistake!
:::

# Section 2 - Customizing Plots

One of the best things about Plots.jl is how easy it is to customize your plots. Let's explore some options:

```{julia}
#| eval: true
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of 10 random values drawn as a red dashed line with a circle marker at every point, titled Customized Line Plot: line style, colour and markers are changed from the defaults."
x = 1:10
y = rand(10)

custom_plot = plot(
    x, y,
    title="Customized Line Plot",
    xlabel="X-axis",
    ylabel="Y-axis",
    line=(:dash, 2),  # Dashed line with width 2
    color=:red,       # Red color
    marker=(:circle, 8)  # Circle markers of size 8
)

display(custom_plot)
```

# Section 3 - Adding Multiple Series to a Plot

Now, let's learn how to add multiple data series to a single plot:

```{julia}
#| eval: true
#| fig-alt: "Line plot with two series of 20 random values each, drawn in different colours and named Series A and Series B in the legend, titled Plot with Two Series."
x = 1:20
a = rand(20)
b = rand(20)

multi_plot = plot(
    x, a,
    title="Plot with Two Series",
    xlabel="X-axis",
    ylabel="Y-axis",
    label="Series A"
)
plot!(multi_plot,
    x, b,
    label="Series B"
)

display(multi_plot)
```

::: {.callout-note}
The `plot!()` function (with an exclamation mark) adds to an existing plot instead of creating a new one. In addition, we used the label here to add a legend to the plot. Remember how we switched the legend off with `legend=false` in Section 1? With multiple series, labels and the legend are exactly how the reader tells the series apart.
:::

# Section 4 - Saving Plots to Files

Plots.jl supports saving your plots to various file formats including PNG, SVG, and PDF, enabling you to use your plots outside of Julia. The function to save plots is `savefig()`: the first argument is the plot itself and the second argument is the file path as a string. The file extension (`.png`, `.pdf`, `.svg`, ...) determines the format. For example:

```julia
savefig(plot_name, "path/filename.png")
```

This saves the plot as a PNG file.

# Section 5 - Advanced Plotting Techniques

Let's explore some other common plot types. While you don't have to solve any task here, the code might come in handy later on during the course as recipes you can copy.

## Bar Plot

```{julia}
#| eval: true
#| fig-alt: "Bar plot with four bars for the categories A, B, C and D with the heights 15, 23, 18 and 30, titled Bar Plot Example."
# Bar plot
x_categories = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]
y_values = [15, 23, 18, 30]
bar_plot = bar(
    x_categories,
    y_values,
    title="Bar Plot Example"
)
display(bar_plot)

```

## Histogram

```{julia}
#| eval: true
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of 1000 normally distributed random numbers in about 30 bins, titled Histogram Example: a bell shape centred near zero."
data = randn(1000)
hist_plot = histogram(
    data,
    bins=30,
    title="Histogram Example"
)
display(hist_plot)
```

## Box Plot

```{julia}
#| eval: true
#| fig-alt: "Four box plots side by side for the groups 1 to 4, titled Box Plot Example. The boxes shift upward from group to group, because each group's random values are centred on its group number."
# Box plot
group = repeat(1:4, inner=50)
y = randn(200) .+ group
box_plot = boxplot(
    group,
    y,
    title="Box Plot Example"
)
display(box_plot)
```

# Section 6 - The Course Look

The plots above use the defaults of Plots.jl. They are correct, but a reader should get their point at a glance. Four rules from the [plotting lecture of our Python course](https://beyondsimulations.github.io/Introduction-to-Python/lectures/lec_09_plotting.html) get you most of the way:

- **The title states the point**: "Category D sells most" says more than "Bar Plot Example".
- **Every number axis has a label with its unit**, for example *Sales (units)*.
- **Bars start at 0**: a bar shows its number by its length, so a cut axis distorts the comparison.
- **Quiet everything that is not data**: no frame, light grid lines, grey labels, calm colors.

The later tutorials share one style for this, called `course_style`.

{{< include ../include/plot_style.qmd >}}

Here is the bar plot from above in the course look:

```{julia}
#| eval: true
#| fig-alt: "The bar plot from above in the course style: four slate-blue bars for the categories A to D with the sales 15, 23, 18 and 30 units, titled Category D sells most: 30 units. The y-axis is labeled Sales (units) and starts at 0, with light horizontal grid lines and no frame."
course_bar_plot = bar(
    x_categories,
    y_values;
    title="Category D sells most: 30 units",
    xlabel="Category",
    ylabel="Sales (units)",
    legend=false,
    course_style...,
    linecolor=course_style.background_color,
    size=(800, 400)
)
display(course_bar_plot)
```

The three dots after `course_style` unpack all of its settings into the call, as if you had typed each of them. You can add more settings after it, like `size=(800, 400)` here, and if one of them is already in `course_style`, the one after it wins. `course_style.background_color` reads a single setting back, so the gaps between the bars match the background.
